body.text: After Tuesday’s Reserve Bank decision to hike the official cash rate, Katy Gallagher took her turn doing the round of media interviews. With calls mounting to meet persistently high inflation with deeper spending cuts, the pressure was starting to show.
“You get a lot of free advice around cutting government spending, but… not so much detail on where and how,” the finance minister declared on ABC24 on Wednesday morning.
Complaining about free advice by suggesting it needs more detail can be taken as an invitation. But while suggestions aren’t lacking there are no easy pickings among them.

The Australian Council of Social Service is calling for a 25 per cent gas tax and the deferment or cancellation of tax cuts scheduled for next year. It rejects calls for cuts in public spending, arguing they would hurt those struggling the most and wouldn’t tackle the key causes of inflation.

Nevertheless, the calls are rolling in. Australian Chamber of Commerce and Industry chief executive Andrew McKellar says the government must take a long, hard look at some of the costly baked-in spending measures Labor holds dear.

His most hardline prescription involves the demand-driven National Disability Insurance Scheme. After the NDIS hit an annual growth rate of more than 20 per cent early this decade, the then minister Bill Shorten set out a plan to slash that figure to 8 per cent. This year, health minister Mark Butler introduced further controversial changes aimed at reducing the annual rise to 2 per cent, capped until 2030. McKellar argues it’s not enough: he is talking far greater cuts, even ending the scheme altogether.
“I’m sorry to say, we cannot afford it,” he says. “It’s not paying for itself. It’s not even remotely paying for itself.”
That kind of call is likely to attract strong protest from within the disability community, where there is widespread opposition to the changes Labor has already proposed.

For other savings, McKellar nominates introducing a means test for home-battery and electric-vehicle subsidies. He says subsidising childcare without an income-based eligibility test is also unsustainable. But he acknowledges his proposals will be unpopular: “Yes, they are tough. And Labor mightn’t like them because it goes to things they have championed. All of these things — all of them — have to be under significant scrutiny.”

McKellar also wants greater fiscal discipline applied within government generally. “The time has come where we really do have to comply with a more explicit set of fiscal rules which will get the budget back onto a more sustainable [footing] and ensure that we can pay down the growing debt burden,” he says.

The rate rise puts the government under renewed pressure to find greater than normal savings in next month’s Mid-Year Economic and Fiscal Outlook, or MYEFO. While treasurer Jim Chalmers continues to blame the war in Iran and consequently high fuel prices, RBA governor Michele Bullock is pointing to the domestic economy and, more precisely, demand pressures from significant spending in the private and public sectors.

Bullock singled out stubbornly sluggish productivity growth as a core problem. She also said the private investment boom in artificial intelligence data centres and renewable energy infrastructure was putting direct upward pressure on inflation through supply problems in construction. That investment underpins key government ambitions around the energy transition and getting Australia a piece of the AI boom, so there’s little appetite at the top to discourage either.

Prime minister Anthony Albanese has designated some other programs as no-go areas. “We won’t rip money out of health or schools,” he said from the sidelines of the unfortunately-timed Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting in Antigua.

“What we will do is take responsible action and take hard decisions,” he said. “We’re the first government to take the decisions that we have on the NDIS. We’re trying to find savings as well, in order to fund aged care going forward. My government will continue to look for all of those measures because we understand that fiscal policy requires that.”
A renewed hunt has begun to identify new ways to boost productivity and save money. But quarantining the biggest-spending areas means turning over a great many other hollow logs.

The government is reluctant to seek significant savings in health or aged care — on which the government wants to boost spending, given demographic trends — or from pensions or social support. It had to drop a plan to cap individual veterans’ allied health support services at $5000 annually after the Senate blocked it. The Senate also doesn’t like a government plan to raise $3 billion over four years by scrapping the extra subsidies over-sixty-fives get towards private health insurance — a cohort most likely to need to use it and already paying more than everyone else, especially if they’ve had it less than a decade and are paying the hefty aged-based levy under program known as “lifetime health cover.” The current subsidy for those people only covers a fraction of the extra they’re forced to pay.

Defence is also deemed out of bounds, despite demands from sections of Labor’s traditional support base to remove the protective fiscal ring fence and take a hard look at outlays, especially projected spending on the AUKUS nuclear submarine program.

The day after the rates decision, the committee that conducted the recent community-generated public inquiry into AUKUS released its findings at the National Press Club. Two of the inquiry’s key figures, former Labor minister Peter Garrett and former defence force chief Chris Barrie, told journalists that a defence deal containing no guarantee of delivery and costing at least $368 billion over forty years — not to mention an estimated $180 billion to store nuclear waste and allegedly unspecified hundreds of billions more on waste disposal — is unacceptable.

“After carefully considering all the material presented to us, we conclude that AUKUS is the worst, most costly and riskiest defence decision ever made by Australian governments, and without adequate public scrutiny,” their report says. “AUKUS represents a massive cost for submarines that are of contested utility and may never arrive. In essence, AUKUS undermines our sovereignty, risks our national prosperity, distorts our defence budget and fails to promote regional peace.”

Independent economist Saul Eslake says political reality means government is unlikely to tackle defence or the other biggest-spending portfolios. Adding in the interest bill on debt, he calculates that they collectively account for almost 60 per cent of federal spending.

“I struggle to see how you could make cuts in the other 40 per cent that would offset the increase in the 60 per cent,” Eslake says. He is a leading critic of the generous Commonwealth deal with Western Australia, struck by the Turnbull government in 2018 and continued by its successors, that boosts that state’s share of distributed revenue from the goods and services tax, to the extreme displeasure of other states.

For starters, Eslake insists the WA deal should be wound back. He also supports calls to means-test the EV and battery subsidy schemes, though he argues childcare is in a different category because it has a multiplier effect as a gateway to greater participation in the workforce, especially for women.

Eslake’s out-of-the-box proposal to drive down inflation involves legislating to give the RBA an alternative to what Albanese has called the “blunt instrument” of higher interest rates. He would give the bank the power to use compulsory superannuation contributions to control how much money is circulating in the economy in order to restrict or boost what income-earners have to spend.

Rate rises place the fiscal repair burden disproportionately on mortgage holders, he says, when it should be spread more evenly across the working population. “I think more people are starting to say: ‘isn’t this unfair?’ Why not give the RBA the power to vary the compulsory superannuation rate?”

How would this work? The RBA would be given legislative authority to tweak the percentage of income that’s compulsorily diverted into super, currently set at 12 per cent. It would increase it slightly when the economy needs cooling and reduce it a little when it needs a boost to consumer spending, never allowed to adjust more than one percentage point above or below the designated official setting.

Because the measure would affect every person being paid super in Australia, small adjustments could have a big impact. “A quarter-per-cent increase would take a similar amount of spending power out of the economy as four quarter-percent rate rises,” he reasons, with the key difference being that the money remains as savings, not payments to someone else.
“It’s still your money and you will get it back with a return on it,” he stresses. And it wouldn’t contribute to distortions in the housing market as interest rate movements can do.

Among the other proposals put forward by different groups, Eslake supports a gas tax but not until oil prices fall, and mindful of the risk of angering customer countries on which Australia relies. He also favours an inheritance tax, to which successive Australian governments have been politically averse. He believes interest rates would be lower now if the Albanese government had deferred delivery of its modified version of the Morrison government’s stage-three tax cuts, pleading economic circumstances.

His bottom-line call is for more honesty and courage in political decision-making. “No one’s got the cojones to say to people: ‘If you want all this extra spending, you’re going to have to pay for it’.”

ANU economics professor and former RBA board member Warwick McKibbin’s diagnosis of Australia’s inflation problem rests on significant private-sector investment and high levels of government spending having created a short-term “demand shock.” The productivity growth that could have counteracted those shocks has been absent and oil-price crisis have made them worse.

Speaking to ABC Radio National on Friday, McKibbin took a dig at politically motivated priorities and pork-barrelling, including “golf courses and other spending programs coming from electoral promises,” which he suggested didn’t help.

“What politicians should be doing — they should have a list of what spending programs have high financial returns or high social returns, rank them and then cut off the ones which are really not performing in the interests of Australians,” he said.
Like others, he was confident there were plenty of savings possibilities, if only political leaders were willing. “It’s really up to politicians to grasp the nettle and actually do their job.” •
